$comment: Configuration template for the legal pack. `agency add legal` copies it to <project>/.agency/legal.json and fills in what it can detect. This file is owned by the PROJECT — a pack upgrade never overwrites it.

repo.$comment_slug: owner/repo. Filled in from the git remote.

brief.$comment: WHAT TO LOOK AT. The method is the same everywhere, the assignment is not.
brief.$comment_default: The standing brief: what holds for this project in every run — what the product does, which relationships it creates, what has already been decided with a lawyer. `agency brief legal --set "…"` writes it here.
brief.$comment_scenarios: Named briefs for repeated sessions, e.g. {"dac7": "January reporting readiness, seller side only"}. Run one with `agency run legal --scenario dac7`.

business.$comment: WHO YOU ARE. This block is the applicability gate — it decides which regimes are even in scope. Guessing it wrong is how a review produces obligations that do not apply to this company, which is the single most expensive failure mode of this pack. `business.model` and `business.size` are required; `agency doctor` reports them as missing.
business.$comment_model: marketplace | eshop | saas | app | content. marketplace = you intermediate contracts between third parties (this turns on P2B, DSA and DAC7 questions). eshop = you sell your own goods. saas/app = you provide your own digital service. Pick the one that describes who the contract is actually between.
business.$comment_size: micro | small | medium | large, per Recommendation 2003/361/EC (micro: <10 staff and ≤ EUR 2M; small: <50 staff and ≤ EUR 10M). Not vanity — DSA Articles 19 and 29 and the accessibility act hang off it. If you do not know, put the headcount and turnover in `sizeBasis` and let the review derive it.
business.$comment_sizeBasis: e.g. "6 staff, ~18M CZK turnover 2025". Free text; the review shows its derivation in the finding.
business.$comment_markets: ISO country codes you actually sell into. Adding a market adds its consumer law — do not list markets you only dream about.

counterparties.$comment_businessUsers: true when third-party professionals offer their goods or services to consumers through you (sellers, instructors, hosts, drivers). This is what turns on the `partners` and `tax-reporting` dimensions, not the word 'marketplace' in the pitch deck.

contracts.$comment_recurring: true when you have long-term obligations to repeated performance of the same type — subscriptions, memberships, standing seller accounts. § 1752 of the Civil Code only ever applies to these.
contracts.$comment_digitalService: true when the consumer gets access to digital content or a digital service over time (§§ 2389f and following). This is what makes the § 2389q change rules apply — a one-off purchase of a physical thing is not it.
contracts.$comment_facilitatesPayments: true when money for the underlying transaction flows through you. Relevant to DAC7 reporting fields and to payment-service questions.

business.$comment_counsel: Who signs off. A named lawyer or firm, or null. The review never replaces them — it prepares the questions and the evidence so their hour is spent on the hard part.

documents.$comment: WHERE THE LEGAL SURFACE LIVES IN THIS REPOSITORY. Findings are anchored to files; a document the pack cannot find is a document it cannot review. Paths are POSIX, relative to the project root. Globs are allowed.
documents.$comment_terms: Audience → path, e.g. {"consumer": "content/legal/vop.md", "instructor": "content/legal/vop-lektor.md"}. Two audiences in one document is itself worth a finding when the duties differ.
documents.$comment_cookiePolicy: Only if it is a separate document. null when it lives inside the privacy policy.
documents.$comment_versionsDir: Where past wordings are kept, e.g. "content/legal/terms/". This is an internal evidence store, not a public archive — see the skill. null means the project keeps no versions, which is a finding in its own right when contracts are concluded electronically.
documents.$comment_acceptanceRecord: Where the project records WHICH wording a given user got — a table, a migration, a model, e.g. "db/schema.sql#user_terms_acceptance". This is the thing that answers 'what applied to this contract' and it is worth more than any archive page.
documents.$comment_other: Anything else with legal content: {"ADR notice": "app/footer.tsx", "instructor payout terms": "docs/payouts.md"}.

product.$comment: WHERE THE CODE IMPLEMENTS THE DOCUMENTS. A promise in the terms that no code keeps is the most common finding this pack produces, and it can only be made if both halves are pointed at.
product.$comment_consentCode: Paths that record or enforce agreement, e.g. ["app/signup/**", "lib/consent/**"].
product.$comment_cookieBanner: The banner component and, if separate, the place that actually gates the scripts. A banner that asks and then loads regardless is a finding, not a detail.
product.$comment_notifications: How the product reaches users on a durable medium — mail templates, notification service. A change mechanism that has no delivery route is not a mechanism.
product.$comment_sellerData: Where seller identity, tax numbers and payouts are collected and stored. Only meaningful when counterparties.businessUsers is true.
product.$comment_dataStores: Schemas or models holding personal data, e.g. ["prisma/schema.prisma"]. Used to check what the privacy policy claims against what the product actually keeps.

posture.$comment: HOW STRICT THE OUTPUT IS. The reason this pack exists: general models default to the most defensive reading of every rule and produce obligations nobody has. This block is the dial.
posture.$comment_level: proportionate = report only what a named provision requires, plus what the product's own promises require of it. conservative = additionally report defensible best practice, each item labelled as such and never scored as a legal requirement.
posture.$comment_requireCitation: true = a finding without a citation to a specific provision, guidance document or the project's own document is dropped before scoring. This is a gate, not a style rule — it is what keeps invented duties out.
posture.$comment_flagOverCompliance: true = report where the product does more than the law asks (re-consent walls, blocking modals, collecting data no rule needs). Over-compliance costs conversion, and data collected 'to be safe' is data you now have to protect.
posture.$comment_assumeWorstCase: false = when a regime's applicability is genuinely unclear, say so and write down what would settle it, instead of applying it. true = apply it anyway. Leave it false unless a lawyer asked for the defensive sweep.

lawSources.$comment: WHERE THE LAW IS LOOKED UP. Primary sources only — both of these are free, need no key, and return the text the courts read. Details and working recipes are in the skill's references/sources.md.
lawSources.$comment_esbirkaOpenData: Czech Collection of Laws as linked data, addressed by ELI: /cz/sb/<year>/<number>/<version-date>. The state-guaranteed consolidated wording.
lawSources.$comment_esbirkaPortal: The human-readable portal for the same ELI. This is what a finding links to — a reader must be able to open the provision.
lawSources.$comment_cellar: EU law by CELEX number through the Publications Office. Content negotiation gives the Czech wording; eur-lex.europa.eu itself does not answer scripted clients.
lawSources.$comment_allowedDomains: Legislators, regulators and courts. A law firm's blog may point you at a provision; it is never the citation.
lawSources.$comment_offline: true = do not go online; work from references/cz-eu-baseline.md and say in every finding that the wording was not re-verified. An offline run is a legitimate outcome, a silently stale one is not.

memory.$comment: The project's memory, not the pack's. Pages are OKF concepts in the knowledge bundle (`type: Page`, `status`, `stale_after`), so a conclusion that stopped holding can be marked instead of deleted. A project that already has this directory elsewhere keeps it — the path below is what the core reads. Which regimes apply here and what has already been decided belongs to the project — that is what stops the next run from re-litigating the same question.
memory.$comment_register: The applicability register: regime → applies here? → why → who decided → when. The most valuable file this pack produces.
memory.$comment_decisions: What the company decided to live with, and on whose authority. A risk that was accepted once must not come back as a finding every month.

review.$comment: The shared output policy — every pack has this block: which dimensions run, what threshold a finding must clear, what language it is written in.
review.$comment_dimensions: Add "partners" and "tax-reporting" yourself once the project has business users — `agency config legal --set review.dimensions='["terms","consumer","privacy","over-compliance","partners","tax-reporting"]'`. They are deliberately not switched on by the installation: running a marketplace regime against an e-shop is how a review produces duties nobody has. Fewer dimensions is a legitimate outcome, not a failure.
review.$comment_minScore: Higher than the reviewer's 80 on purpose. A wrong legal finding is not a wasted five minutes — it gets a product changed, a checkbox added and a conversion rate dropped for a rule that was never there.

sinks.$comment_runRecord: Always true. The run record is the truth, everything else is a derived sink — if a sink fails, the finding is not lost.
